dedupe_keys.name: flint water crisis 2014 to 2016 lead corrosion and the water infrastructure crisis behind it

description: This case study is the Virginia Tech Flint Water Study team's December 2016 explanation of the water infrastructure crisis that lay behind the 2014 to 2016 Flint public health crisis in Michigan. It reports that, by late 2016, data from the EPA, CDC, the state environment agency, Virginia Tech and other universities placed Flint's water in the range of other US cities for lead, disinfection by-products and bacteria, while residents were still advised to use lead filters. The article then asks why residents of the second poorest large US city paid some of the highest water rates in the world, and gives three reasons: a system built for 250,000 people now serves under 100,000, slow water in oversized pipes accelerates corrosion, and deferred maintenance compounds costs. It weighs bottled water, lead pipe replacement and main upgrades as spending choices and argues for outside funding. The team produced it as part of citizen science work with residents. Coverage: one city, 2014 to 2016, with a narrative and tables of water rates, not a dataset. Access: a free web article; the licence is not stated. Caveats: it is an advocacy-informed synthesis, not a peer-reviewed study, and its figures come from the cited agencies. It informs infrastructure ageing, service-line replacement and utility financing models, and relates to the EPA SDWIS drinking water system records in the catalogue.

outcomes: Showed that a source switch without corrosion control released lead from ageing service lines, and that a shrinking customer base, slow-moving water and deferred pipe replacement made the wider infrastructure crisis worse and costly.
